Read About Agra

A Mughal capital that moved on, leaving behind the empire's most famous monument to grief.

THE CAPITAL THAT KEPT MOVING

Agra was the seat of the Mughal Empire for most of a century, but no single emperor treated it as permanent. Akbar made it his base and then, in 1571, built an entirely new capital at Fatehpur Sikri 40 kilometres away — only to abandon that one within fifteen years when its water supply failed. His son Jahangir and grandson Shah Jahan both governed from Agra, but Shah Jahan shifted the capital again in 1648, this time to a new walled city in Delhi. Agra never fully recovered its political standing after that, which is part of why its Mughal-era core survives so intact: the city stopped being rebuilt over.

Fatehpur Sikri was a functioning imperial capital for less than fifteen years. It has looked essentially the same, empty, for the four hundred since.

A MONUMENT BUILT FOR ONE DEATH

Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to her and Shah Jahan's fourteenth child, on campaign in the Deccan. The Taj Mahal that followed took an estimated twenty thousand workers and roughly two decades to complete, and it is a tomb before it is anything else — every proportion of the white marble mausoleum, the char-bagh garden and the twin red-sandstone buildings flanking it was set by the requirements of a single grave. Shah Jahan's own end was less generous: his son Aurangzeb deposed him in 1658 and held him under house arrest in Agra Fort for the last eight years of his life, in rooms positioned so he could see the tomb he had built across the river but never visit it again.

THE DRESS REHEARSAL ACROSS THE RIVER

Itmad-ud-Daulah's Tomb predates the Taj Mahal by roughly three decades and is widely read as its design draft. Empress Nur Jahan commissioned it in 1622 for her father, and it was the first Mughal structure built entirely in white marble rather than red sandstone, the first to use pietra dura — semi-precious stone inlaid into marble in floral patterns — at scale, and the first to abandon the fortress-like bulk of earlier tombs for something closer to a jewel box. Every element the Taj Mahal is famous for had already been tried here first, at a fraction of the size.

Agra's UNESCO World Heritage List entry is unusual: the city holds three separate sites — the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri — inscribed individually rather than as one combined listing.

WHAT SURVIVES WHEN A CAPITAL LEAVES

Fatehpur Sikri is the clearest illustration of what an abandoned Mughal capital looks like: a complete red-sandstone city — palace complex, mosque, private quarters, administrative halls — standing almost exactly as the court left it in the 1580s, because nobody with the money or the motive to alter it ever moved back in. The Jama Masjid there, entered through the 54-metre Buland Darwaza gateway, still holds the white marble tomb of the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, whose blessing Akbar credited for the birth of the heir he had been unable to produce elsewhere — the reason the capital was built on that spot in the first place.

PETHA AND THE CITY BEHIND THE MONUMENTS

Agra's most distinctive food has nothing to do with the Mughals: petha is a translucent candy made from ash gourd, a vegetable with almost no flavor of its own that takes on whatever it is cooked in — sugar syrup, saffron, fruit essence. It has been made in the city's Sadar Bazaar lanes for generations and is sold by weight from shopfronts that look unchanged by the tourism economy fifteen minutes away. The gap between the two Agras — the monument circuit built for a few hours' visit and the ordinary city of two million people who live there year-round — is one most visitors never cross, though it starts just outside the ticket gates.

MANAGING THE CROWDS

The Taj Mahal now runs on a ticketing system built almost entirely around throughput: a foreign-visitor entry fee that bundles a small bottle of water and shoe covers, a Friday closure that exists because the complex still functions as a mosque, and an East Gate queue that consistently moves faster than the West and South gates because it is where foreign-ticket holders are funneled. A separate toll, run by the Agra Development Authority, charges foreign visitors once for same-day entry to five of the city's monuments together — a single administrative fix for a UNESCO city that receives several million visitors a year but was never built, physically, to process them.
